extracted.intended_audience: Australian Government policy makers and agency drafters preparing Impact Analyses and consultation plans
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for Australian Government agencies on designing, conducting and documenting stakeholder consultation as part of the Policy Impact Analysis process. Covers when to consult, who to consult, consultation methods, planning, assessment and OIA expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine and timely consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy makers should consult in a genuine and timely way with affected people, businesses, community organisations, and other policy makers to avoid creating cumulative or overlapping impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine consultation process ensures real‑world impacts of policy options are considered and leads to better outcomes and greater understanding, particularly among those adversely affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Analysis consultation section requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The consultation section of the Impact Analysis must: explain the purpose and objectives of consultation; outline a plan for conducting consultation; outline the principal views of stakeholders; summarise key areas of agreement and areas of difference; describe how the preferred option has been modified to take account of stakeholder views or why dissenting views have not been adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five points are mandatory content for the consultation section and are what OIA expects to see documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation before final decision (required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact Analysis will be assessed as insufficient if no consultation has taken place prior to a final decision, including consultation with other policy makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation should normally occur before final decisions; if consultation was not done, justify why and note risk of an 'insufficient' assessment by OIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation to inform consideration of all viable options
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation plays an important role in ensuring every practical and viable policy alternative has been considered and feedback on all genuine and viable options should be reflected in the Impact Analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders may suggest useful solutions; Impact Analysis should reflect the feedback received on all genuine options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess distributional impacts through consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation is particularly important for understanding the potential distributional impacts of proposed measures across the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stakeholder input to identify how impacts are distributed across different groups (e.g., small vs large businesses, regions, vulnerable populations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation options and default
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four consultation options: full public, targeted, confidential or post-decision. Full public consultation is the appropriate level for all proposals unless there is a compelling case for limited consultation (e.g., market sensitivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose consultation type proportionate to the proposal's impacts; be prepared to justify a more limited approach to OIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co‑design processes and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where co‑design processes are used, drafters must discuss the range of views presented and demonstrate that parties in the co‑design provide a representative voice for the range of views that may be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May still need to consult stakeholders outside the co‑design if other strong views exist; co‑design does not replace broader consultation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult other policy makers and regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consult relevant Australian, state/territory and local government agencies and regulators to avoid creating cumulative or overlapping regulatory burdens and to ensure policies can be administered consistent with Government intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intergovernmental consultation identifies existing settings, overlapping functions, and opportunities to streamline or minimise burden; regulators and service delivery agencies often hold useful implementation and customer data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous consultation (start early, continue throughout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation with key stakeholders should be continuous and should start as early as possible, continuing through all stages of the policy development cycle, including when detailed design features are being finalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early consultation (e.g., before Early Assessment) helps define the problem, objectives and options; continuous engagement helps identify potential problems and reduce regulatory capture risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad‑based consultation (capture diversity of stakeholders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the scope of proposed changes and consult widely so consultation captures the diversity of stakeholders affected (general public; businesses; consumers; unions; environmental groups; state/territory/local governments; Australian Government bodies; international partners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between stakeholder subgroups where impacts differ (e.g., by business size, location); do not rely solely on peak bodies where they may not represent all relevant stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business stakeholder engagement (associations vs individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: For business stakeholders, industry associations and small business groups are a starting point, but they might not represent all stakeholders; consider best ways to engage individual stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large industry associations may have diverse memberships; consider engaging individual firms and use ASBFEO as a resource for small business consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible consultation materials and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation should ensure stakeholders can readily contribute: inform them by appropriate means; present information in plain language with summaries; publish documents online to increase accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use easy-to-comprehend formats, summaries, website publication; consider support strategies for stakeholders who lack resources or capability to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of consultation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation can take forms other than written submissions such as stakeholder/public meetings, working groups, focus groups, surveys or web forums. Appropriateness depends on issues, groups and time available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine methods (online and traditional) to maximise reach and accessibility; online tools can complement formal processes and increase interactivity (social media, GovTEAMS, blogs, wikis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise burden on stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultations should not be burdensome: conduct early, set realistic timeframes, avoid unreasonable demands on stakeholders (especially small businesses and individuals), and coordinate with other agencies to reduce repeated burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid holiday periods and end of financial year; where stakeholders face frequent consultation, consider joint consultation with other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent objectives, scope and decision context
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear about consultation objectives, the context for them, when/how final decisions will be made, and what aspects are already final and not open to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state assumptions and areas where input is sought; make documentation (draft Impact Analyses, white/green papers, exposure drafts) available to enable informed comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and show how feedback was considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Show stakeholders how consultation responses have been taken into account; welcome and respond to feedback even if not adopted; use the Impact Analysis to provide information on consultation responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissenting views should be dealt with respectfully and explained in IA if not adopted; publish consultation statements within the IA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent but flexible consultation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent procedures to ease stakeholder participation and coordination, but be flexible where public consultation is inappropriate (e.g., national security, commercial-in-confidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential consultation can be used case-by-case; OIA can advise on appropriate level of consultation—consult OIA early in policy development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and review consultation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy agencies should evaluate their consultation processes and continue to examine ways to make them more effective (e.g., use ICT to improve cost-effectiveness and timeliness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation can include number/types of responses, which methods succeeded, accessibility outcomes, and how responses affected decisions; OIA encourages publishing consultation protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow adequate time (not rushed) — typical durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide realistic timeframes for consultation; meaningful consultation timelines generally range between 30 to 60 days, with 30 days considered the minimum, though timing depends on proposal significance and stakeholder capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer rounds for whole-proposal consultations or when stakeholders have limited resources; allow time for organisational clearance (boards, management) for large organisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation as a means not an end
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation should improve decisions, not substitute for making decisions; additional consultation is not required in Impact Analysis if other legislative consultation requirements have been met and are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'over‑consulting' or consulting for consultation's sake—but ensure quality and proportionality are maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and criteria for consultation types
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear criteria for when each consultation type is appropriate: Full public (with all affected parties; transparent); Targeted (parties most directly affected; publicly available); Confidential (discreet, commercial-in-confidence, case-by-case); Post-decision (after initial decision but before implementation, focused on implementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use table of appropriateness (Table 1) to justify choice to OIA; post-decision consultation should only be used where pre-decision consultation would undermine effectiveness and confidentiality is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation strategy and planning elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A consultation plan should cover the whole policy making process and identify objectives of consultations, relevant target groups, appropriate forms of consultation and consultation times, proportionate to the potential impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing a consultation plan improves transparency and gives stakeholders early warning; emphasis should be on high-quality consultation rather than quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round-specific planning: objectives, participants, forms, timing
rubrics_metrics.description: For each consultation round, identify: what the objective is (co-design, gather ideas, validate assumptions, clarify impacts), who will be consulted, what form consultation will take, and when it will commence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different rounds may target different elements of Impact Assessment (problem, objectives, options, impacts, whole proposal); informal stakeholder contact before written consultation is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure drafts for complex legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Release exposure drafts of complex policies before finalisation to test implementation details and allow businesses and stakeholders to provide detailed comments on how the law will apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure drafts help verify stakeholder understanding of legal rights/obligations and may identify opportunities to simplify proposed laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIA assessment questions and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: OIA will assess consultation in Impact Analysis by asking: Does the IA explain the purpose/objectives of consultation (before final decision)? Does it have an appropriate plan for consulting those affected? Does it demonstrate that views of affected stakeholder groups have been considered?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIA pays particular attention to whether options suggested during consultation have been included or discussed; final assessment evaluates transparency and appropriateness at each stage (reference Table 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: International trade/WTO notification obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed regulation may impact international trade, consider whether notification under WTO agreements (TBT, SPS) is required and notify early enough for Member comments to be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify early in development; consider TBT for technical/product requirements and SPS for measures protecting human/animal/plant life or health; contact points provided for inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish consultation protocols and include consultation statement in IA
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are strongly encouraged to publish consultation protocols on their websites and include a consultation statement in the Impact Analysis documenting meaningful consultation throughout policy development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consultation statement demonstrates to decision makers and the public that sound consultation practices were followed and explains how responses affected the final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online tools thoughtfully to increase interactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Online consultations can range from simple websites for submissions to interactive tools using social media or collaboration platforms (GovTEAMS) and can be open or closed depending on needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online methods can complement traditional methods and improve accessibility; choose interactivity level appropriate to the information sought and confidentiality needs.
